newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hits China's plan to disband HK legislature.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hits China's plan to disband HK legislature.

text.p: The United States, supporting Britain, said on Friday that China's plan to disband Hong Kong's elected legislature when Beijing takes back the territory next July was "unjustified and unnecessary".
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten denounced China's plans on Friday and proposed letting the World Court rule on the dispute.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns called the Chinese plan a "very worrisome development" and said the United States supported "open, accountable and democratic government in Hong Kong".

"The United States has frequently expressed both publicly and privately our view that disbanding the current elected legislature in Hong Kong is unjustified and unnecessary," Burns told a news briefing.

After more than 150 years of British rule, the territory of 6.3 million people falls back under the Chinese flag at midnight next June 30, with promises from Beijing's communist leadership that almost nothing will change.
At that moment, a Beijing-appointed legislature will take over from the elected Legislative Council (Legco), reversing democratic reforms introduced by Patten over the past four years.
Burns said both Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs Winston Lord had made the U.S. point recently to Chinese leaders.
Some 400 wealthy and influential Hong Kong people picked under China's supervision will meet in the Chinese frontier city of Shenzhen on Saturday to elect a provisional legislature.

"China has said ... that a provisional legislature will not operate for more than one year," Burns said. "The United States believes a legislature elected on the basis of open and fair elections should be put place as soon as possible."
"The United States will watch closely what action a provisional legislature takes and how that legislature lasts."
Washington believed that stability in Hong Kong's governing structures was vital to ensure its continuing growth, success and prosperity after 1997, he added.
